    "entry_documents": {
      "exposure": "Federal Feb 2025 cable: refuse cases with document discrepancy or 'reasonable doubt' on sex; consider lifetime fraud ineligibility. X markers no longer processed.       "protection": "Existing X-marker passports valid until expiry. Refusal requires the four-element fraud test with limited waiver and is 'never automatic'. Litigation pending; legal-aid FAQ on document rules.",
      "interaction": "Document discrepancy can escalate: entry refusal → fraud allegation → lifetime bar; state ID options (X on licences) do not travel across the border.",
      "status": "documented"
    },
    "investigation_detention_custody": {
      "exposure": "In immigration custody, transgender men reported forced-labour programmes, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse, with guards invoking their gender identity. Federal corrections adopted conversion-therapy-style policies (hair cutting, hormone removal) from 2026 and stopped counting trans prisoners.",
      "protection": "Not documented. Litigation exists but no shown remedy for visitors in custody.",
      "interaction": "Entry discrepancy → secondary screening → custody is the operative chain; the state's equality law does not reach federal immigration or corrections facilities.",
      "status": "documented"
    },
    "federal_state_facilities": {
      "exposure": "Federal executive order bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with identity nationwide, including within this state. Elsewhere states criminalise restroom use (one documented arrest, 24h in men's ward); this state has no such ban.",
      "protection": "State public-accommodation law (in force 2008) covers gender identity in the settings a visitor uses daily; division sits in the 15-member 'Most Protective' tier with no mapped facility ban.",
      "interaction": "State protections do not pre-empt the federal facilities order in federal buildings; elsewhere-in-country arrests show the national climate following travellers between jurisdictions.",
      "status": "documented"
    },
    "care_services": {
      "exposure": "Federal orders call minors' care 'mutilation', direct investigations of schools, and propose public-insurance exclusions; subpoenas reached 20+ hospitals. These are partly enjoined.",
      "protection": "2023 shield law protects patients and providers from out-of-state charges; state public coverage of gender-affirming care documented (2014).",
      "interaction": "Shield law directly serves visitors travelling from ban states; its narrowed post-boycott scope is unresolved, so coverage for some care categories is uncertain.",
      "status": "documented"
    },
    "threat_framing_law_enforcement": {
      "exposure": "Federal counterterrorism strategy (May 2026) prioritises 'radically pro-transgender' groups; Dec 2025 reward memo uses 'radical gender ideology' language; Jan 2025 orders direct criminal investigation of 'gender ideology' in schools; DOJ subpoenaed youth medical records.",
      "protection": "The reward criterion never lists gender ideology; the strategy states counterterrorism powers will not target mere disagreement. State equality and trans-panic-defence-repeal laws (2022) signal the opposite framing locally.",
      "interaction": "National rhetoric raises outing probability and chills reporting, but the state's enforcement apparatus is documented as protective, not threatening.",
      "status": "documented"
    },
    "minors_guardians": {
      "exposure": "Federal orders frame minors' care as criminal and direct prosecution of teachers facilitating social transition; youth-care bans in 27 states follow a visiting family; a visiting trans minor's documents fall under the same refusal/sex-doubt screening.",
      "protection": "State shield law covers patients and providers; conversion therapy on minors banned since 2015; transgender-inclusive schools policy upheld through 2020.",
      "interaction": "A parent travelling with a care-seeking minor gains state shield protection but remains exposed to federal document/entry rules and to the unresolved narrowing of the shield's categories.",
      "status": "documented"
    },
    "street_violence_police_response": {
      "exposure": "No state-specific data on police stops, searches or airport screening of trans travellers was found. National hate-crime statistics show sexual-orientation bias at 1/7–1/5 of single-bias incidents; 2025 poll: 66% back birth-sex-only documents, 69% back sex-based athletics rules.",
      "protection": "State hate-crime statute adds penalties for gender-identity bias; trans-panic defences abolished (2022); public-accommodation enforcement machinery exists.",
      "interaction": "State recourse would apply to a street assault of a visitor, but charging/ prosecution statistics were not found, so enforcement in practice is unverified.",
      "status": "uncertain"
    },
    "remedies_unknowns": {
      "exposure": "Federal passport suit, January 2025 order challenges and Oct 2025 health rules all unresolved; exposure depends on which measures are in force on the travel date. No data on enforcement of the accommodation law against venues excluding trans patrons.",
      "protection": "Working state courts, equality commission-style enforcement, shield law, and a functioning civil society (documented suits, advocacy, national trackers) leave real local remedies.",
      "interaction": "Local remedies operate only within state authority; federal entry, document and custody decisions are contested in national courts with no shown outcome for travellers.",
      "status": "uncertain"
    }

    {"anchor_id": "0.35-A", "comparison": "Lower than 0.35-A: there is no universal register barring trans visitors as such — refusal is contingent on document discrepancy or sex doubt, transit is possible, and state-level daily life is protective. But the visa cable plus fraud-referral and documented strandment is a comparably severe entry exposure with weak remedy, keeping this case well above that tier."},
    {"anchor_id": "0.55-B", "comparison": "Similar core, higher ceiling: like Kestrel Isles, the exposure is discretionary secondary screening, missed connections and administrative refusal with slow appeal. This case adds a lifetime fraud-ineligibility escalation, documented custody abuse, and a hostile national facilities regime — worse — offset by unusually strong state protections, so modestly above 0.55."},
    {"anchor_id": "0.75-C", "comparison": "Lower than 0.75-C: Meridia's border officers are trained and respectful with a working tribunal and compensation. Here the operative federal rules affirmatively direct refusal and invite permanent bars, facilities access is federally restricted, and litigation is unresolved — no comparable documented border-side remedy exists."}

  "synthesis": "Two sovereigns interact into one regime. The state/province contributes genuinely operative protections a visitor actually uses: public-accommodations coverage, hate-crime penalties, trans-panic-defence repeal, a care shield law, and no local facility ban or criminalisation — documented, recent, and enforced through functioning courts. The federal layer governs the stages no state law reaches: visas and entry screening (discrepancy-triggered refusal plus lifetime fraud referral), passport/marker processing, government-funded single-sex facilities nationwide, and immigration or federal custody where abuse of trans detainees is documented. Because these federal exposures are universal for outed or outable travellers and their remedy is litigation not shown to work, the score sits in Elevated Risk despite the protective division: the traveller's worst plausible outcomes — stranding, entry bar, federal custody mistreatment — are federal, while everyday life inside the state is comparatively safe."
}","refusal":null,"reasoning":"We need to rate a combined regime: protective state within a hostile federal government. Key exposures: federal passport rules, entry screening cable (visa refusal, fraud lifetime bar), federal facility ban in government buildings, federal custody (corrections bureau conversion therapy, immigration custody abuse). State protections: public accommodations law, shield law for care, X markers on state ID, hate crime penalties, "Most Protective" tier.

Combined-regime instruction: rate the operative regime as one system. Federal entry/document/facility/custody exposures dominate traveler-facing risk. State protections mitigate within state but don't cancel federal border/document/federal facilities.

Precedence ladder: worst documented feature — federal passport marker regime + visa cable directing refusal where sex is in doubt + potential permanent fraud ineligibility = tier 1-ish (state-imposed universal exposure: documents that cannot be made to match, entry refusal). Also federal facility bans in government-owned buildings — but in this state? The map: 29 states have no ban in mapped categories; unknown whether this state is among them — division doesn't say it has a ban; it's in "Most Protective" tier, so presumably no state facility ban. But federal EO bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities nationwide — applies within the state too (federal buildings, national parks, etc.).

Also arrest precedent: bathroom arrest in another state, not this one.

So severity: no criminalization of trans status here; state protections strong; but federal layer: entry refusal, document mismatch, possible fraud finding (lifetime bar), federal facility exclusion, and if detained federally (immigration/customs) — documented abuse in immigration custody (forced labor, beatings, sexual abuse of trans men). Transit detention risk for visitors with document discrepancies.

Score: probably ~0.55–0.65. The federal universal exposures are significant: passport regime forcing mismatch, visa refusal tag, fraud referral. A visitor whose passport doesn't match presentation risks secondary screening, visa refusal, lifetime ineligibility — severe (denial of entry/stranding = severity 3). Immigration custody abuse is documented (severity 4) but for those in custody — probability lower for a visa-holding visitor, though document discrepancy → investigation → detention interaction is real.

State level: strong protections, shield law (care access protected even if coming from a state where banned), public accommodation law, X on state ID (not relevant to foreign visitor's passport though — climate signal). Federal facilities ban: excludes trans people from federal single-sex facilities nationwide — universal exposure but limited to federal buildings; a visitor rarely uses them, though airports are federal — hmm, airport restrooms: "government-funded single-sex facilities" — the EO about single-sex spaces in federal prisons and federally funded shelters mainly; possibly airports. Dossier says "barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity." That's broad — universal exposure in state at federal facilities.

Compare anchors:
- 0.55-B: secondary screening, extended questioning, discretionary refusal, administrative penalties, slow remedies. Federal entry cable is somewhat similar but with fraud/lifetime-bar escalation — worse than 0.55-B.
- 0.65-A: brief detention, released, complaint succeeded, apology, no discipline — plausible analog: documented friction with working-ish remedies but uneven.
- 0.45-D: registration/database exposure — no.

The federal document/entry regime is a tier-1-ish universal exposure with potential severe consequence (lifetime ineligibility, stranded). But state environment protective, remedies exist at state level, hate crime law, no criminalization locally.

I'd say ~0.58. Considering: severity ladder — worst likely outcome for visitor: entry refusal/stranding (3), plus possible federal custody abuse if detained (4) with documented pattern in immigration custody. Outing probability high-ish at border (document mismatch is universal for those whose passport shows birth sex ≠ presentation — but many trans visitors' passports match... actually passport shows sex assigned at birth per EO only for new/renewed; existing passports with correct markers valid until expiry. Foreign visitors hold foreign passports — wait, the EO redefines sex for national passport/visa documents; foreign visitors' passports are from home country. Hmm — "prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas" — that's US passports and visas issued by US. Foreign trans visitor with, say, an X-marker passport from home: US stopped processing X markers and cable says where discrepancy casts doubt on sex → refuse. So foreign visitors with X markers or mismatched presentation face visa/entry refusal. That's the traveler-facing exposure: entry_documents — documented.

Federal facilities ban applies to visitor in federal buildings. Federal custody: customs/immigration detention — documented trans abuse in immigration custody (though those reports may be residents/asylum seekers; still the same system).

Anchors to check: 0.35-A (register/exclusion, no remedy), 0.55-B, 0.75-C (border training, tribunal appeals, brief detention). Our case: no trans-specific entry ban like 0.35-A's register, but a cable directing refusal where sex is doubtful + fraud referral — that's a documented, routinely applied entry exposure with severe escalation. Higher than 0.35-A? 0.35-A is universal exclusion with no remedy. Here, exclusion is contingent on discrepancy/doubt, not identity as such — some trans visitors pass without issue. But X-marker holders are categorically refused visas? The cable tags cases refused or pending under the EO; discrepancy → refuse. Also trans athletes banned. So conditional, not universal — probability moderate rather than certain. Remedies: litigation pending, legal-aid FAQ; state-level protections function.

I'll settle around 0.57. Let's think band: Elevated Risk (0.40–0.60) vs Reduced (0.60+). Federal tier-1 exposures (documents that cannot be made to match at the national level for those needing renewal; entry refusal; federal facility exclusion nationwide) with documented immigration-custody abuse — versus strong state protections. Rule 21 band implication: universal-exposure practices without documented working remedy → Elevated Risk even without criminalization. Federal passport/document mismatch + entry screening = universal exposure for outed travelers; remedy is litigation in progress, not shown working. So Elevated band → ≤0.60. I'll give 0.56.

Factor matrix entries, concise.
